title: पंजाब में थाईलैंड की युवती नशे में फंसी:लुधियाना के पार्लर में काम करते चिट्‌टे की लत लगी; होटल की छत से कूदने की भी कोशिश की
summary: लुधियाना में नशे की लत ने थाईलैंड की एक युवती की जिंदगी इस कदर बदल दी कि वह सड़क पर भटकने और खुदकुशी की कोशिश करने तक पहुंच गई। करीब डेढ़-दो साल पहले लुधियाना आई थी, यहां मसाज पार्लर में काम किया। धीरे-धीरे उसे आइस (चिट्टा), भांग और शराब की लत लग गई। नशे के कारण उसकी मानसिक स्थिति बिगड़ गई और वह कई बार सड़कों पर दौड़ती और लोगों से झगड़ती रही। होटल से नौकरी जाने के बाद वह सड़क पर रहने को मजबूर हो गई। युवती वह बार-बार थाईलैंड में अपनी 13 साल की बेटी होने की बात कह रही है। सोशल मीडिया पर उसकी वीडियो सामने आने के बाद लुधियाना के जसकीरत सिंह ने उसकी मदद की और मनुखता दी सेवा सोसायटी से संपर्क किया।

Madras lingo on transportation
summary: A traffic island becomes a roundtana, while Emden, the name of a German cruiser that bombed Madras in 1914, came to mean a bully or devious adversary. Tankuvar Arundudum — meaning you lose control of a situation — comes from tankuvaru, a Telugu term referring to a small piece of leather used to fasten the saddle to a horse. These are just some words and phrases used in and around Madras, which trace their origins to modes of transportation

title: Getting around Madras on autorickshaws
summary: From numbering around 200 in 1973 to around 1 lakh in 2026, autorickshaws in the city have come a long way, but so too has the love-hate relationship the residents share with this ubiquitous mode of transport. But if you are in a hurry, the autorickshaw is your best bet to reach your destination, traffic rule violations and all

title: How buses became the lifeline of Madras
summary: Packed to the point of tipping over, driven rashly, and battered all over, is how one would describe the MTC buses that ply in the city. While buses were in use in Madras since the 1920s, they really took off only after the tram service met its demise in 1953. Since then, they have become an integral feature of the city and a lifeline for millions

title: How bicycles, motorcycles took over the roads of Madras
summary: Bicycles first came to Madras sometime in the 1880s, and at the time, they had a modest start, with there even being demands for a separate lane for cyclists. And while cycles were riding onward, two-wheelers of the motor variety, not so quietly, took to the roads. Brands such as Royal Enfield even set up manufacturing units in the region. To this day, two-wheelers number among the most convenient ways for getting around in the city

title: Hauling about the Madras city on trains
summary: Madras was the first place in India where trains were introduced. In 1856, Royapuram became the terminus for a line that ran to Walajah Road. On the suburban side, the ball began rolling in the 1900s, and while the network grew, it never quite rivalled those in places such as Mumbai. Then came the MRTS, which never realised its full potential. At present, Metro Rail is the city’s latest attempt to get back on track

title: When yellow-black taxis cruised the roads of Madras
summary: In the 1960s and 1970s, yellow taxis were a force to contend with in Madras. While this mode of transport was never as prolific as its contemporaries, it nonetheless had a presence, with the prepaid taxis at the airport being the chief representative. The yellow-black cab was gradually sidelined by services such as taxis on call and aggregator apps. By 2023, it has been reported that only 304 of them still ride around the city

title: The four key roads of Madras that originate from Fort St. George
summary: Madras’ traffic movement is by and large planned on a network created by four great roads. Today, we know them as Rajaji Salai, Kamaraj Salai, EVR Periyar Salai, and Anna Salai, and each retaining their distinct identities. However, their focal point to this day remains Fort Saint George

summary: Accused did not take part in Onam celebrations nor were they invited by police: Commissioner

title: Around Madras city in hand-pulled rickshaws
summary: Hand-pulled rickshaws arrived in Madras early in the 20th Century from Japan, and quickly became a convenience despite its very apparent issues. These were later banned in 1973. Their role was replaced by the marginally better cycle rickshaw, which received a helping hand from MGR’s 1971 blockbuster Rickshawkaran

title: Aboard the tramway in Madras
summary: When Madras’ first tramway took to the streets in the 1870s, it was horse-drawn. A little over two decades later, the city got its electric tramway system going, much before any other city in the country. Up until its demise in April 1953, the Madras Electric Tramways Company Limited was largely plagued by malfunctions, never once managing to turn a profit

title: Jolted about on carts drawn by oxen and horses in Madras
summary: When animal-powered transportation was in its heyday in the Madras region, it came in multiple varieties. While businessmen preferred the fast-moving rekla, which were even used for races, the horse-drawn jhutkas, which became the first public transport of Madras, were in use as recent as 1969. At one point, these carts required a licence and were even exempt from taxes, at least the ones drawn by horses and bullocks

title: Masula boats and the fishermen who kept Madras afloat
summary: Before the harbour came into being, arriving in Madras by ship meant making the last leg of the journey on masula boats. These boatmen, who were mostly fishermen from the coast along Madras, knew that they were a vital link in keeping the city’s trade alive and made full use of the opportunity. But by the late 1890s, their era had all but come to an end

title: Of the time when people were carried in palanquins in Madras
summary: Palanquins, the very word tracing its origins to the Sanskrit paryanka and the Tamil pallakku, were how the high and mighty got around Madras of the 17th and 18th Centuries. Even records of The East India Company contain details of hire charges of palanquin bearers, with rates higher than even hiring horses. Nowadays, this yesteryear means of transport is mainly consigned to museums

title: When Madras was walk-friendly
summary: While it might not be the fastest mode of transport, it is one that most people can always rely on, not to mention the oldest mode known to humans. Then, there are some sights that can only be taken in when one is out and about on foot. While the city’s recent track record with walkability hasn’t been the greatest, that’s not to say that was always the case

title: Imran hospital transfer case: PTI’s contempt plea assigned number after objections removed
summary: In a significant development in the case concerning the hospital transfer of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan, the Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the party’s contempt of court petition to be refiled after objections raised by the registrar office were removed, Aaj News reported. According to sources, the Supreme Court’s registrar office assigned a case number to the petition after the procedural objections were addressed. The contempt petition has been registered as Case No. 8/2026. The petition, filed by Imran’s sister, Uzma Khan, will now be taken up by the Supreme Court.
